explanations.answer: Ignoring every voice and every correction
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Zephaniah says she "…heeded no voice…" and "…accepted no correction." (Zephaniah 3:2). Not one voice got through, and not one correction either. I've had dough that listened better than that.

explanations.answer: Listening but keeping her own ways
explanations.explanation: Close, but listening is the part she skipped. Zephaniah says she "…heeded no voice…" (Zephaniah 3:2). That means nobody got through to her at all. She wasn't hearing people out and then doing her own thing.

explanations.answer: Waiting for a sign from heaven
explanations.explanation: Nope, the verse never has her waiting for a sign. It says she "…does not trust in the LORD; she has not drawn near to her God." (Zephaniah 3:2). Trusting and drawing near are what the verse says she lacked.
I get why you'd hope so, friend, but the text says the opposite. Zephaniah says "she has not drawn near to her God." (Zephaniah 3:2). She didn't trust in the LORD either. So this one is false.
Yes, false. Zephaniah says she "…does not trust in the LORD; she has not drawn near to her God." (Zephaniah 3:2). No trust and no coming close. That's a long way from where a city ought to be.

explanations.answer: They leave nothing for the morning
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Zephaniah says her judges are "…evening wolves, leaving nothing for the morning." (Zephaniah 3:3). These were the people who were supposed to be judging fairly, and that's what makes it sting.

explanations.answer: They keep watch through the night
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a good wolf, but it's not this one. A watchman guards the place. These wolves devour it, and they're "…leaving nothing for the morning." (Zephaniah 3:3). Nothing about guarding in that picture, friend.

explanations.answer: They only hunt when times are hard
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the text doesn't hold back the hunting for hard times. The picture is wolves at evening who leave "…nothing for the morning." (Zephaniah 3:3). It's about how thoroughly they take, not when they take it.

That's it, baker. "Her prophets are reckless, faithless men." (Zephaniah 3:4). A prophet is supposed to speak for God, so reckless and faithless is about the hardest thing you could say about one. I'd want the nearest exit too.

That would be a sad story, friend, but it's not this one. Zephaniah calls them "…reckless, faithless men." (Zephaniah 3:4). Faithless is the opposite of faithful. The problem was with the prophets themselves, not just with people ignoring them.
Not quite, baker. Zephaniah calls them "…reckless, faithless men." (Zephaniah 3:4). Wise and reckless don't sit together in that description. Silent isn't a word the verse uses about them.

I wish that were so, friend, but it's the other way around. Zephaniah says the priests "…profane the sanctuary…" (Zephaniah 3:4). Profane means they treat the holy place as if it were ordinary. So this one is false.

You've got it. The priests "…profane the sanctuary; they do violence to the law." (Zephaniah 3:4). They were supposed to protect what was holy, and they did the opposite. Priests who treat the sanctuary like a regular room is a hard thing to hear.

Yes, baker. "The LORD within her is righteous; He does no wrong." (Zephaniah 3:5). Look at the setting. The lions, the wolves, the reckless prophets and the priests are all there, and the LORD is right in the middle of it, and He is righteous. That's the steady part of this whole passage.

explanations.answer: Weary and ready to leave her
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, friend. It says the LORD is "within her" and that He "…does no wrong." (Zephaniah 3:5). Nothing there about being weary or leaving. He's right there, and He's righteous.

explanations.answer: Patient but looking the other way
explanations.explanation: Not looking away at all. The verse says "He applies His justice morning by morning…" (Zephaniah 3:5). That's a LORD who is paying attention and doing right every day. Looking the other way doesn't fit that, baker.

explanations.answer: They feel no shame at all
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The verse says "…the unjust know no shame." (Zephaniah 3:5). The LORD within her is righteous and does no wrong. He applies His justice morning by morning and does not fail at dawn, and still the unjust feel no shame.

explanations.answer: They hide from Him in fear
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd think so, but the verse doesn't say that. It says "…the unjust know no shame." (Zephaniah 3:5). Hiding would at least be some kind of reaction. Here there's no shame at all.

explanations.answer: They start to turn back to Him
explanations.explanation: That would be a happy ending, friend, but the verse doesn't say that. Zephaniah says "…the unjust know no shame." (Zephaniah 3:5). Nothing there says they start turning back, even though "He applies His justice morning by morning…"

Yes, "fear." The LORD says, "I said, ‘Surely you will fear Me and accept correction.’…" (Zephaniah 3:7). Fear goes right alongside accepting correction in His words. Then the verse says "…they rose early to corrupt all their deeds."
Not "leave," baker. The LORD said, "Surely you will fear Me and accept correction." (Zephaniah 3:7). It's about her turning toward Him and letting Him correct her, not walking away.
Good try, friend, but it's not "test." The LORD said, "Surely you will fear Me and accept correction." (Zephaniah 3:7). The word is "fear," and it goes right alongside accepting correction.

That's right. The LORD says that if she feared Him and accepted correction, "…her dwelling place would not be cut off…" (Zephaniah 3:7). The text puts those two things side by side. It's like a recipe where you can see what happens if you follow it.

Not false, friend. The LORD says, "Surely you will fear Me and accept correction." Then "…her dwelling place would not be cut off despite all for which I punished her." (Zephaniah 3:7). So the text does say it, and the answer is true.

That's it. The LORD says He will "…pour out upon them My indignation—all My burning anger." (Zephaniah 3:8). That's the end of the verse's list, and it's heavy. This is a serious line, so read it slowly.
I wish it were, friend, but the verse says something else. The LORD says He will "…pour out upon them My indignation—all My burning anger." (Zephaniah 3:8). The word is anger, and it's a heavy one.
Riches would be a very different verse, baker. The LORD says He will "…pour out upon them My indignation—all My burning anger." (Zephaniah 3:8). What gets poured out is His anger, not riches.

Yes. The LORD is the one speaking, and His words end with "…all the earth will be consumed by the fire of My jealousy." (Zephaniah 3:8). It's a serious ending to a serious passage. I'll let His words stand just as they are.

A flood is a good guess, because the Bible does have one (Genesis 7:17). But that's not this verse. Here the LORD says "…all the earth will be consumed by the fire of My jealousy." (Zephaniah 3:8). It's fire this time, friend.
Good guess, but not here, baker. The LORD says "…all the earth will be consumed by the fire of My jealousy." (Zephaniah 3:8). What does the consuming is fire, not hunger.
